prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the strongest case I can make on the criteria I apply as an instrument builder and as Chair. The magic-wavelength lattice is a sharply defined new technique: it removes Doppler and recoil shifts while interrogating thousands of atoms at once, and it took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18. The result has been reproduced independently in many national and university laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL), and clock-to-clock comparisons over fibre are routine, which is the kind of independent confirmation I ask for. It already delivers tests of fundamental constants, millimetre-scale relativistic redshift measurements and a pending redefinition of the SI second, and it is a clean two-person attribution (Katori for the concept and first demonstration, Ye for taking it to record accuracy). Six of eight members rank it in the top three, with three first places, so it is the nearest thing to a convergent candidate on this list. My own opening first choice, IceCube (B046), remains a discovery I rate very highly, but I no longer think it is the best vehicle for a consensus this year.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is precision-measurement technology developed in a lineage the Academy has recognised twice: Hall and Hansch for the frequency comb in 2005 and Wineland and Haroche for single-quantum-system control in 2012. A sceptic can say the lattice clock is a refinement rather than a new door. Attribution is also not airtight, since Ludlow, Takamoto, Lemonde, Pottier and others contributed and are outside the two credited names. The citation must therefore be drafted to say precisely what is new: the magic-wavelength many-atom lattice, and not combs or ion clocks. I also accept that a redefinition of the second has not yet happened, although I do not think scientific recognition should wait for it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as a new measurement technique, but says the citation must be handled carefully relative to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and notes that Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and others are not credited.
responses.response: I agree on both points and I think the overlap concern is the main risk to this candidate. Where I would press further is that the distinction is concrete: a comb gives you the ruler, and an ion clock gives you one quantum absorber, while the magic-wavelength lattice gives you many atoms at once, which is what delivers the stability and the 1e-18 systematics control. I would put that in the citation. On the uncredited groups, I accept that Katori and Ye is a pragmatic two-name unit, but I would ask the committee to confirm in the background review that Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and 2005 Sr demonstration have clear priority over the parallel lattice-clock work in Paris and Boulder.

responses.point: Danielsson puts baryon acoustic oscillations first as a clean discovery from nature that turned dark energy into a measured expansion history, and ranks the lattice clock third, asking whether it is discovery or instrument development.
responses.response: I share your admiration for BAO and I ranked it third myself. My difficulty is attribution and recency of cosmology prizes, not merit. The 2005 detection came from two large survey teams, SDSS and 2dFGRS, and the underlying physics was predicted decades earlier by Peebles and Yu and by Sunyaev and Zeldovich, so a Eisenstein-Cole-Peacock trio looks more like a choice among many than a natural fit. On your discovery-versus-instrument question, I disagree that it should count against the clock: the Academy's own phrase is 'discovery or invention', and a measurement technique that moves a limit by two orders of magnitude and enables new physics tests meets that bar. I would keep BAO as a strong future candidate rather than push it this year.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first, as a quantitatively predicted state of matter with confirmed experiments and very large influence, and calls the recognition arguably overdue.
responses.response: This is outside my expertise, so I rely on you and Mehlig here. I take the point that it is mature and influential, and that is why I name B045 as an alternative. My concern is the credit structure rather than the physics: you yourself note that the Kane-Mele phase does not occur in real graphene, that Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang (with Zhang deceased) predicted the HgTe system, and that 3D credit (Hasan, Moore, Balents, Fu) is split off. Three colleagues propose Kane, Mele and Molenkamp while Olsson proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan. Before I could support it as the top choice I would want the committee to agree on whether the prize is the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or topological insulators generally, and the 2016 prize on topological phases also needs a clear distinction in the citation.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the lattice clock first as a sharply defined invention underpinning geodesy and tests of constants, and ranks IceCube eighth because it is collaboration-scale, with only a few sources identified and limited independent confirmation from KM3NeT and Baikal.
responses.response: The criticism of IceCube is fair on attribution: it is a roughly 300-person collaboration and AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal were precursors. I would answer that the diffuse flux itself is confirmed by several independent IceCube analyses and increasingly consistent cross-checks, and the Nobel tradition has rewarded instrument leaders in collaboration-scale discoveries when the conception and leadership are identifiable, which they are for Halzen and Karle. I still concede that independent confirmation by another detector is thinner than for the clock, and that is a legitimate reason to rank it below B022 today. We agree on B022 and on the clean two-person credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the lattice clock is distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and how to word the citation to make that distinction.
Priority and credit for the magic-wavelength concept and first Sr lattice clock among Katori, Ye, and groups such as Lemonde, Ludlow and Takamoto, which expert review should settle.
Whether IceCube credit can be cleanly limited to Halzen and Karle, and whether independent confirmation from KM3NeT or Baikal will strengthen by the time of the decision.
Whether the committee prefers a two-part prize pairing a measurement-technology achievement with a different field, which I have not proposed because the 3-person cap would force a split of credit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the lattice clock, optical clocks, topological or cold-atom candidates. I work in astroparticle physics and cosmic-ray and gamma-ray instrumentation (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur) and have no recorded collaboration with IceCube, BAO survey teams or the named individuals. I flag that my field adjacency to B046 and my first-place ranking of it should be weighed by colleagues, as should my role as Chair.
